newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Russia release decades of data on Arctic.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Russia release decades of data on Arctic.

text.p: Volumes of long-classified information on the Arctic Ocean unveiled on Tuesday by Russia and the United States hold keys to better understanding global climate change and other environmental questions, Vice President Al Gore said.

As an outgrowth of cooperation between Gore and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, the two countries released a CD-ROM of data gathered over five decades on the region they once thought could be a prime battleground of the Cold War.

Gore told a news conference at the National Geographic Society the CD-ROM -- the first of several -- doubles the available oceanographic information on the region. The society participated in the project to release the data.

"Over the years the former Soviet Union and Russia and the United States have amassed vast quantities of data about virtually every corner and every crevice of the Arctic. But for military reasons this potential treasure trove of information remained strictly off limits," Gore said.

With the Cold War's end, Gore and Chernomyrdin agreed to work to release data gathered by the U.S. Navy and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute in St. Petersburg, Russia.

What was produced was an atlas of the region that included 1.4 million observations made by Russian scientists on winter conditions in the eastern Arctic, which was forbidden territory to Western scientists during the Cold War.
More CD-ROMs are planned on data on summer conditions, Arctic ice and meteorology. The information also will be available at the NOAA site on the World Wide Web at http://ns.noaa.gov/atlas.

"We do know that buried in these hundreds of thousands of observations can be found clues to the puzzle of climate change, which I believe is one of the most important challenges we face as we enter the 21st century," Gore said.

Scientists are eager to learn more of the interplay between ocean currents and temperatures, which are greatly influenced by the Arctic, and the world's climate, which is being affected by the build-up of carbon gases in the atmosphere from burning fossil fuels such as coal and oil.
"With this collection and through our collaboration today some of scientists' most sought-after data literally has come in from the cold," Gore said.

Gore has long raised warnings of global warming. In findings consistent with global warming models, he noted, NOAA researchers have found the percentage of annual preciptation that falls in intense storm events such as the recent rains in the U.S. West has increased by 20 percent.

Gore and other U.S. officials at the briefing said the information also will be key to learning how nuclear waste dumped by the former Soviet Union and other pollution that has accumulated in the Arctic environment is transported by currents and how better to deal with it.
